rationale: Intermediate-horizon momentum skipping the most recent week to avoid short-term reversal; underreaction to news (Jegadeesh & Titman 1993; Indian evidence in Sehgal & Balakrishnan 2002).
Risk-adjusted (Sharpe) momentum: trend scaled by its own volatility is less crash-prone and more persistent (Barroso & Santa-Clara 2015; Blitz, Huij & Martens 2011 residual momentum).

Low-volatility anomaly: leverage-constrained and lottery-seeking investors overpay for volatile stocks (Ang et al. 2006; Frazzini & Pedersen 2014 betting-against-beta; Joshipura & Joshipura 2016 for India).
Proximity to recent high: anchoring makes investors underreact to good news near highs (George & Hwang 2004 52-week-high momentum, here with a 3-month high).
MAX/lottery effect: stocks with extreme recent daily gains are overpriced by lottery-seeking (retail-heavy) investors and subsequently underperform (Bali, Cakici & Whitelaw 2011).
Average intraday range as an idiosyncratic-volatility proxy; high-IVOL stocks underperform (Parkinson 1980 range estimator; Ang, Hodrick, Xing & Zhang 2006 IVOL puzzle).
Amihud illiquidity: price impact per rupee traded earns a liquidity premium (Amihud 2002), slow-moving enough for a monthly hold.
One-month reversal from liquidity provision and overreaction at monthly horizon (Jegadeesh 1990; Lehmann 1990), strong in emerging markets with heavy retail flow.
Variability of trading activity: stocks with volatile turnover earn lower returns (Chordia, Subrahmanyam & Anshuman 2001).
High-volume return premium: abnormal trading activity raises visibility and investor recognition, followed by higher returns (Gervais, Kaniel & Mingelgrin 2001; Merton 1987).

Close location value (Chaikin accumulation/distribution): persistently closing near the day's high indicates end-of-day buying pressure from informed/institutional traders (market practice; cf. Lou, Polk & Skouras 2019 on intraday vs overnight clienteles).
Price-volume co-movement: rises on swelling volume signal attention-driven chasing that later reverses (Lee & Swaminathan 2000; WorldQuant 101 Alphas, Kakushadze 2016).

Rising delivery share signals accumulation by position-taking investors rather than intraday speculators (NSE delivery-volume market practice; informed-trading interpretation in Indian studies of delivery data).
High average delivery share indicates a long-horizon, information-based investor base and less noise-trader mispricing (Indian market practice; cf. Barber & Odean 2008 on noise-trader concentration).
Delivery-weighted momentum: returns earned on high-delivery days reflect committed capital and information, so they persist (cf. Llorente, Michaely, Saar & Wang 2002 on informed vs hedging volume).
Speculation-weighted return: price moves driven by intraday squared-off volume are noise and reverse over the following month (Llorente et al. 2002; De Long et al. 1990 noise traders).

Positive correlation between returns and delivery share means buying is done by holders taking delivery (accumulation) while selling is speculative, a bullish flow signature (Wyckoff/OBV practice; Llorente et al. 2002).
Surge in rupee delivered value measures fresh institutional/investor capital entering the stock, an under-reacted demand shift (Gervais et al. 2001 adapted to delivered volume).
Delivery share at the top of its own 3-month range flags abnormal accumulation relative to the stock's normal speculative mix (time-series anomaly practice).
Standardised abnormal delivery share: a z-score version of accumulation comparable across stocks with different baseline delivery levels.
Volatility per unit of delivery: volatility produced by speculative intraday trading rather than investor repositioning is mispricing-prone and lottery-like (Ang et al. 2006; Bali et al. 2011).
Stable delivery share means a stable holder base; erratic delivery reflects episodic speculative bursts that precede underperformance (Chordia et al. 2001 liquidity-variability analogue).
Accumulation divergence: delivery share rising while price falls indicates patient buyers absorbing supply, preceding recovery (Wyckoff accumulation / OBV divergence practice).
Momentum confirmed by high delivery: trends backed by committed holders underreact and persist, while low-delivery trends are speculative (Lee & Swaminathan 2000 volume-momentum interaction).

Persistent futures premium above carry reflects leveraged long demand that cannot be arbitraged under cash short-sale constraints, i.e. overpricing (Miller 1977; Ofek & Richardson on constrained arbitrage).

Abnormal basis relative to the stock's own norm isolates speculative futures demand from structural carry; excess optimism reverses (Miller 1977; Stambaugh, Yu & Yuan 2012 sentiment-driven overpricing).
Rising futures premium indicates informed traders using leverage in futures first, as futures lead spot in price discovery (Chan 1992; Indian evidence in Thenmozhi 2002).
Unstable basis signals arbitrage stress and investor disagreement, associated with overpricing and later underperformance (Miller 1977; Diether, Malloy & Scherbina 2002 dispersion).
Elevated put open interest relative to calls reflects informed bearish positioning in options, which predicts lower stock returns (Pan & Poteshman 2006; Cremers & Weinbaum 2010).

Short-term spike in PCR relative to its norm marks fear extremes and put-writer support levels, a contrarian sentiment signal in Indian F&O practice (cf. Simon & Wiggins 2001 on contrarian sentiment indicators).
Rising put/call open interest over a month indicates accumulating bearish informed positioning (Pan & Poteshman 2006; Johnson & So 2012 option-to-stock activity).

Positive return/OI-change correlation means price rises come with new longs (long build-up) and falls with unwinding, the bullish build-up pattern used in Indian F&O practice (cf. Bessembinder & Seguin 1993 on OI and price).

Open-interest build-up signed by price direction: long build-up (OI up, price up) is bullish, short build-up (OI up, price down) bearish (NSE F&O market practice; Hong & Yogo 2012 on OI predictive content).
Monthly long build-up vs short build-up in rupee open interest: new leveraged capital agreeing with the price move signals informed conviction (Hong & Yogo 2012; market practice).

Futures positioning crowded relative to cash liquidity marks leveraged speculation and MWPL/ban risk, followed by weaker returns (crowding literature, e.g. Lou & Polk comomentum; SEBI market-wide position limit practice).

Price gain not explained by growth in futures leverage indicates cash-market (fundamental) demand that persists, whereas leverage-driven rallies unwind (cf. Brunnermeier & Pedersen 2009 funding-driven prices).
